info.name: PANDA Docker API
info.description:
Field-level encryption for personal data, over HTTP.

## Before you start

Import the environment template next to this collection, then set:

- `baseUrl` — your own PANDA deployment. There is no shared public endpoint; every organization runs its own instance.
- `apiKey` — a key issued by that deployment, prefixed `panda_svc_`. Mark it as a **secret** variable type in Postman so it does not appear on screen during a demo or a screenshot.

If the deployment runs with `PANDA_AUTH_MODE=mtls+apikey` — the production default — you also need a client certificate. Postman takes that under **Settings → Certificates**, with the host set to your `baseUrl` host. Without it the connection is refused before the API key is ever read.

## Running the requests in order

`Encrypt` stores the envelope it receives, and the decrypt requests read it back. Running the collection top to bottom walks the whole round trip and leaves you with a working example of each call. Running a decrypt request on its own will fail, because nothing has been encrypted yet in this session.

## Masking is the default

`Decrypt` returns a masked value such as `32************01` — safe to put in an API response or a log line. Reading the full plaintext is `Decrypt to the full plaintext`, which requires the `unmask` scope and is audited on every call. When its test fails with 403, the credential does not hold that scope; that is the intended answer, not a defect.

exec: // Reachable without credentials on purpose: an operator debugging a
// deployment needs to ask what is running before they can authenticate
pm.test('reports the service and the SDK it links against', () => {

request.description: What this instance is running. No credentials required, deliberately — an operator debugging a deployment needs to be able to ask what is running before they can authenticate against it.

exec: // The wire format is fixed by panda-spec, and every SDK reads it.
// Asserting the shape here is what turns this from documentation into
// a contract test: a change that breaks interoperability fails now,
// rather than in an organization's PHP application six months from now.
pm.test('the envelope does not contain the plaintext', () => {
// Kept in two forms on purpose. `envelopeJson` is the JSON-escaped
// string, ready to drop into a request body without its quotes
// breaking the surrounding JSON; `envelope` is the readable original.

request.description:
Produces a PANDA envelope — a JSON string holding the ciphertext and the metadata needed to read it back.

Store it as-is in a `TEXT` column. Do not parse it, and do not size the column for the plaintext: an envelope is roughly 1.34x the plaintext plus about 130 characters of JSON and nonce overhead.

## `kid` is required in practice

Set `kid` in your environment to a key your deployment holds. Omitting it does **not** fall back to a default: the service answers `unknown_kid`, because the key provider resolves a key only from the identifier it is given. The OpenAPI document currently describes the opposite — that is a known discrepancy, recorded rather than papered over here.

Naming the key explicitly is worth doing anyway. It is what makes rotation possible later without re-encrypting everything.

A truncated envelope is the most common cause in practice: a `VARCHAR` sized for the plaintext silently cuts the JSON, and the failure surfaces here rather than at insert time.

The read path for almost every caller. The masked value is safe to return in an API response, write to a log, or display in a frontend without further protection.

Run `Encrypt` first in the same session — this reads the envelope it stored.

// does not hold the `unmask` scope. Ask for the scope rather than
pm.test('refused: this credential does not hold the unmask scope', () => {
// What answers "who read this citizen's data, and when" during an
// audit. Log it alongside your own request id.

request.description:
Returns the original value. Requires the `unmask` scope, and every call is recorded in the audit log with the caller's API key id and certificate Common Name.

Before reaching for this, consider whether you need to:

- **Display a value?** Use `Decrypt (masked)`. The masked form is usually what the screen should show anyway.
- **Look a record up by value?** Use `Blind index`. That never decrypts anything.
- **Export data?** Ask whether the export needs full values or whether masked ones serve.

If the answer is still yes, this is the right endpoint — and the audit record is how you show the decision was deliberate.

request.description:
Applies PANDA's masking to a plaintext you already have, with no encryption involved.

For an import pipeline, a report, or a migration that holds plaintext from somewhere else and needs the same masking the service would apply on a read.

// the same width — another length means the column truncated it on
// insert, and it will never match on lookup.
pm.test('the index is base64 of a 32-byte digest', () => {
pm.test('the index does not contain the value', () => {
// The mode has to come back, because two systems that normalise
// differently produce different indexes for the same value and then
// never match — with no error to explain it.
pm.test('the normalisation mode applied is reported', () => {

request.description:
A deterministic HMAC index for a value, so a record can be found by exact match without decrypting anything.

Store it in a separate column — conventionally `<field>_bidx` — and query that column:

```sql
SELECT * FROM citizens WHERE nik_bidx = $1;
```

## Choosing `normalization`

The value is normalised before it is hashed. Leave it empty for `lowercase`, or send `nik`, `trim`, or `none`.

**Pick the mode that matches whatever computes the other side of the comparison.** If your application indexes with the SDK, use the mode it passes there. Two systems that normalise differently produce different indexes for the same value, and the search then returns nothing — no error, no warning, just an empty result that looks exactly like a record that is not there. The response reports which mode was applied; log it beside the index you store.

## The index is immutable

It is derived from the value, the index key, and the normalisation. Changing any of the three means re-indexing every row, and rows indexed differently will never match. Decide all three before the first row is written.

## What it leaks

The index is deterministic: two rows with the same value have the same index. For a NIK that reveals almost nothing, because the value is unique anyway. For a low-cardinality field it reveals almost everything — an index on blood type across ten thousand rows is a list of blood types, even though the encrypted column beside it is not. Do not blind-index demographic fields; UU PDP treats religion, gender, marital status and blood type as sensitive on their own.

exec: // Index another value and hand the result to a callback. pm.sendRequest
// does not inherit the collection's auth, so the header is explicit here.
// The regression test for a defect this endpoint shipped with.
// Normalisation used to be fixed to `nik`, which strips everything
// that is not a digit. Any non-numeric value therefore normalised to
// the empty string, and every such value produced one and the same
// index — so this endpoint silently returned a constant for names,
// emails, and anything else without digits.
pm.test('the second value could be indexed', () => pm.expect(err).to.be.null);
pm.test('two different names do not share an index', () => {

request.description:
Two different names, both indexed, and the indexes compared.

This exists because the endpoint once returned the *same* index for every value without a digit in it — a name, an email, a place of birth all collapsed into one. Lookups did not fail; they returned whatever shared that index, which for a whole class of values is every row.

Kept as a test rather than a note, because nothing about the wrong answer looked wrong.

request.description:
A NIK written the way people type it, indexed under the `nik` rule.

`nik` strips everything that is not a digit, so `3201-0125-0199-0001` and `3201012501990001` produce the same index. Without it they would be two different people as far as the database is concerned.

It is not the default, and that is deliberate. `lowercase` cannot empty a value; `nik` can — apply it to a name or an email and it strips the whole thing, leaving every such value sharing one index. Ask for it where it belongs.
